![Illustration by Mario Hugo for The New York Times.](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

The New York Times Magazine put four people who mostly disagree in a room and asked them a concrete question: if you are a college student today, or any worker watching this happen, how should you prepare for the AI future of work? The full discussion is at the Times ([gift link](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/09/magazine/ai-jobs-workforce-labor.html?unlocked_article_code=1.o1A.rDxZ.us30E-Jap_6d&smid=bs-share)). The panel:

- [**Daron Acemoglu**](https://economics.mit.edu/people/faculty/daron-acemoglu), economist at M.I.T. and a Nobel laureate
- [**Dean Ball**](https://www.hyperdimensional.co/), former adviser on AI and emerging technology to the Trump administration, now a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation
- [**Ethan Mollick**](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/), professor at the Wharton School and author of *Co-Intelligence* and the forthcoming *Co-Existence*
- [**Clara Shih**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Shih), former top AI executive at [Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com/) and [Meta](https://about.meta.com/), co-founder of New Work Foundation, a nonprofit aimed at helping entry-level workers navigate AI.

The discussion was moderated by [Bill Wasik](https://www.nytimes.com/by/bill-wasik), editor of the Science desk at the Times. The setting is a season of college commencements where graduates booed speakers who talked up AI, set against entry-level layoffs in the headlines and "learn to code" quietly retired as a guaranteed path.

What follows is a thematic summary of the discussion, with the salient exchanges quoted; the editing and condensing are the Magazine's.

## The "Marcus Chen" problem: how capable, how fast?

The panel keeps returning to one image, from a habit of Mollick's: asking the models to describe their own future. The scenario keeps degrading under his questioning: Marcus Chen (a stock chatbot name for a developer) first "goes into the office" to direct his AI agents; asked why he'd commute when the agents do the work, the model retreats to a beach house he checks in from; pressed on why he'd check in at all, it finally settles on "Marcus Chen sits at the beach. …" The joke sets up the real question, which Mollick states plainly:

> **Mollick:** A lot of this comes down to the question of which kind of world we're in. Is it one where AI is a fairly normal-ish technology and change comes more slowly, or is it a world where AI actually becomes super capable?

His leading example is the one closest to home, programming, where "being a coder" went from "writing good code on a regular basis" to "managing engineering tasks" in the span of months.

Shih takes the beach scenario at face value and asks the obvious follow-up: "He's on the beach, he's having a great life. But what about the other workers? It is now faster, more efficient to have fewer cooks in the kitchen." Acemoglu sharpens it into the question that organizes the rest of the panel:

> **Acemoglu:** How many Marcus Chens can the American economy employ? It's just not realistic to think that 100 million people will work like Marcus Chen.

**The counter-case is Ball's, and it is a case for slowness.** He is bullish on the technology and bearish on the drama:

> **Ball:** The transformation that's coming is going to take place in the world as it is familiar to us today, and every single day will feel familiar. And there'll be tiny, tiny changes along the margin. … And 10, 15, 20 years later, we'll look back and we'll say, *My god, everything is different*. But you'll never notice it happening.

His reasoning is that the jobs everyone worries about are already heavily automated (sending an email, writing code, running a mine), so taking the human out of one more loop is a small slice of the total cost. Acemoglu's rejoinder targets the central assumption of the agent era:

> **Acemoglu:** The current view is that somehow agents are going to do a lot of the work and we just need to supervise them. I find that very unrealistic. But if it *was* realistic, it would be a horrible thing.

Shih, who is in the middle of building a startup, splits the difference from experience. The agent tooling let her incorporate, file IRS and California paperwork, and write a privacy policy in days with almost no staff, work that "in the past, we would have needed to hire dozens of people and engage with multiple external law firms" over months. Her verdict is deliberately two-sided: "AI displacement *is* realistic and real, and it's both horrible and wonderful."

Mollick adds the upside (early GPT-4 work that helped Kenyan entrepreneurs) but Acemoglu immediately names the catch: economics' "excess entry" problem, where cheap access to a profession floods it past the point of being worth anyone's while. And Mollick closes the section with the practical brake on all the disruption talk: the Walmarts and Coca-Colas of the world have no plan to reorganize around agents, "and that gives us time to react."

::: {.callout-note}
**The Kenya study.** Mollick is pointing to [a field experiment](https://osf.io/hdjpk/) that gave small-business owners in Kenya a GPT-4–based mentoring assistant. The headline finding was uneven: high performers improved while low performers did slightly *worse*: the assistant amplified existing skill rather than closing the gap.
:::

## Which jobs, beyond the tech bubble

Wasik pushes the panel out of software, and Shih answers with three personas that extend the question beyond tech. First, the shape of the problem, via Amazon: a million-plus workers, a thin "elite group" of coders and supervisors at HQ, and everyone else in the warehouse or driving, "managed to the minute." Then the two workers nobody puts on a panel:

> **Shih:** Let's talk about Stacey Smith, a hypothetical health insurance claims adjuster. She and millions of people like her are employed in the U.S. in insurance and banking because of regulatory reasons that those jobs could not be off-shored. But now a lot of those approvals, whether it's mortgage underwriting or claims adjusting, are easily done by AI agents … What about Bob Johnson? … He is one of three and a half million truck drivers in the U.S. who again make a decent wage. They live in the South … They are the breadwinners for their family. … What happens when the [Waymo](https://waymo.com/) technology diffuses and we get past regulatory barriers to the Bob Johnsons?

Her point is that the regulatory moat that kept Stacey employed is exactly the kind of barrier agents are built to dissolve, and the geographic concentration means the pain lands hard in specific places.

Ball agrees on the white-collar targets ("consulting, marketing, customer service, entry-level legal work, administrative work … definitely real") but draws two limits. One is preference, not capability: "I'm kind of doubtful that a humanoid robot's going to be making you a cocktail at a bar, even if it could. People don't want that." The other is that a lot of senior knowledge work is really persuasion and internal politics, which he doubts gets automated away.

Mollick points to a Procter & Gamble experiment where AI didn't just speed people up, it dissolved the boundary between roles:

> **Mollick:** Business people used to have business ideas, tech people came up with technical ideas. But add AI, and everyone comes up with ideas in between each other.

::: {.callout-note}
**The P&G study.** This is the field experiment written up as ["The Cybernetic Teammate"](https://www.nber.org/papers/w33641): 776 Procter & Gamble professionals worked real product-innovation tasks alone or in pairs, with or without AI. Individuals with AI matched two-person teams without it, and the commercial/technical role boundary blurred whenever AI was in the loop.
:::

**Acemoglu turns the question around to the sectors that actually move the productivity needle** (manufacturing, health care, education), and argues each is a bottleneck rather than a quick win. Manufacturing automation "requires a huge amount of engineering services" per step; health care's last digitization wave (electronic health records) *lowered* productivity; and education, in his telling, is already the warning: "There's a nice large-scale study coming out from China … which shows horrible, horrible outcomes from students who use AI." His fear is that health care repeats the education mistake: "unleashing chatbots in a way that really leads to horrible outcomes."

::: {.callout-note}
**The education claim.** Acemoglu doesn't name the study, and "coming out from China" doesn't correspond to a specific identifiable paper. The closest documented large-scale evidence that unstructured student AI use harms learning is a high-school mathematics randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Turkey: students given GPT-4 *without guardrails* did worse on later unaided tests, while a guardrailed tutor version avoided the harm [["Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning," *PNAS* 2025](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122)].
:::

Ball and Mollick push back on the framing itself. Ball: "if all we had were chatbots, I would probably share your pessimism. But … the new coding agents are essentially computer programs that can use computers." Mollick goes further ("I don't think we're talking about chatbots anymore") and points to AI outperforming doctors on diagnosis in many settings and to evidence that *structured* AI tutors help even where unstructured use hurts. The disagreement is less about the data than about whether today's failures are intrinsic or a deployment problem we haven't solved yet.

::: {.callout-note}
**Diagnosis and tutoring.** On diagnosis: in a randomized study, GPT-4 on its own scored higher on diagnostic reasoning than physicians did with or without it [["Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning," *JAMA Network Open* 2024](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.40969)]. On tutoring: a physics RCT at Harvard found students learned more from a well-designed AI tutor than from an active-learning class [["AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning," *Scientific Reports* 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6)]. That is the "structured" half of Mollick's point; the "unstructured use hurts" half is the Turkey RCT in the note above.
:::

## Advice for young workers: experience is the scarce input

Asked what to tell a young person, the panel produces the predictable answers and then dismantles them. Ball likes "curious generalists" and the skilled trades: "plumbing and electricians and HVAC technicians." Mollick won't even grant that: "I also don't think we can predict well enough to say, *Go be a plumber*, because then the Plumbot10000 could come out in a couple of weeks." Acemoglu agrees the trades get *more* complex and more valuable, with a caveat that doubles as his thesis for the whole panel: "that's not where the center of gravity of the investments in AI are going."

Shih reframes it as distribution rather than category. From spending her days with 25-year-olds, she sees "a tale of two cities": "Those who know how AI works, specifically AI agents, can get their dream job … Those who don't have those skills, those entry-level jobs are disappearing." Her concrete prescription is to own a side project end to end, because "it is very difficult to then really understand and stay in control of AI if you don't learn something end to end."

Mollick's concern is why the entry-level rung is the one breaking. Judgment is downstream of experience, and experience is what the bottom rung used to provide:

> **Mollick:** What I really worry about with junior workers is that field experience is often crucial to evaluating work you didn't create yourself, whether it comes from humans or AI … Daron or I can look at an academic paper instantly and say whether it's going to be worth an hour of our time to read or not. Dean can scan a piece of AI legislation and spot the loophole. Clara can … look at any bit of code and judge whether it was written by an idiot or an expert. If you have no experience, you can't do those things.

This is the apprenticeship problem, and Mollick names it as such: the model that built that judgment "worked for 4,000 years" and "all collapsed," because firms have stopped hiring the juniors who did the grunt work that the assessment depended on. His one structural hope is that universities are "actually quite good at training and assessing" and could extend professional education into the gap AI is opening.

Two qualifications temper the advice. Mollick, who has assigned side projects for a decade, notes they are "not for everyone": uptake varies sharply by background and socioeconomic status. And Acemoglu rejects the steady state Shih describes as livable. The treadmill of relearning which model does what every quarter just to stay in place is, to him, the tell that something has gone wrong:

> **Acemoglu:** Right now, you have to spend a lot of time learning different models, their capabilities, their shortcomings, and then three months later you have to experiment with lots of different models again in order to just stay where you are. That is absolutely not productive, that's very dystopian. … To me, that's a horrible future.

Shih's answer is the question the rest of the panel is really about: "I said earlier that it's wonderful *and* horrible. How do we make it less horrible and more wonderful?"

## What to do: coordination versus the Industrial Revolution

The policy exchange is where the disagreement stops being about forecasts and becomes about values. Ball, who helped draft the White House's 2025 [AI action plan](https://ai.gov/action-plan/), wants measurement before remedies ("You can't create policy remedies for a problem you don't understand") and is openly hostile to broad consultation:

> **Ball:** Now the pope seems to want us to have a committee of all the AI stakeholders, all the impacted communities. But we didn't create a stakeholder committee for the Industrial Revolution. It didn't unfold by show of hands.

Acemoglu takes the analogy and turns it over to show the underside:

> **Acemoglu:** Yeah, there was no committee for the direction of the Industrial Revolution. And what did we get? In the early stages, we got children working to death in coal mines. Conditions in factories became horrible. Wages for many workers fell. Now AI is changing things much faster and affecting many, many sectors at the same time.

Shih answers both at once: "the lesson isn't that coordination is unnecessary; it's that skipping it costs us decades of human suffering." She adds a legitimacy point: policy "that emerges without broad input will not be trusted, as it will be perceived to represent the agenda of big tech, capital or one political faction."

Ball's own forecast cuts against his preferred policy:

> **Ball:** I don't know what the unemployment rate will be in 2028, but I guarantee you that 100 percent of it is going to be blamed on AI.

His worry is that the backlash produces European-style labor rigidity, enacted not in Washington but across "50 different state houses" while everyone pretends to understand what's happening. Shih reads the same backlash as a reason to act now rather than wait: the [Eric Schmidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Schmidt) commencement reaction, a Gallup poll finding a third of Gen Z describe their feelings toward AI as *anger*, because "these are people we want embracing AI." and instead "they're rejecting it on a moral basis."

Two closing points. Acemoglu's is a design argument against the whole "automate everything" framing: that AI and human intelligence are simply different kinds of thing.

> **Acemoglu:** When two things are different, the last thing you want is to try to mimic one with the other. … They should work together. And those aren't the kinds of models we're trying to develop.

Shih returns to where the panel began:

> **Shih:** The key thing about AI agents is that they all have a goal. And it depends on who deploys it, because whoever deploys it gets to set the goal. … But that's a choice we can make.

The panel splits on speed, on which jobs, and on whether to coordinate. Its one point of convergence is Shih's: the goals AI serves depend on who deploys it.

This panel is that argument in a room that mostly disagrees with him.
- [GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models](/posts/20230321-gpts-are-gpts-labor-market-impact/) — the exposure-estimate counterpart to the panel's "which jobs" question: OpenAI's finding that higher-wage occupations face more task exposure, the quantitative backdrop for the Marcus/Stacey/Bob personas.
- [Agentic Coding Is a Trap](/posts/20260507-agentic-coding-is-a-trap/) — Mollick's apprenticeship worry at the scale of one developer: orchestrating sub-agents trades away the very judgment the orchestration depends on, and that judgment used to be built by doing the work agents now absorb.
- [AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance](/posts/20260528-ai-assistance-reduces-persistence/) — the randomized evidence behind the Acemoglu–Mollick education exchange: ten-minute AI-assisted sessions lowered later unaided performance, with the damage concentrated among users who asked the AI for direct answers (the unstructured-use failure mode).
- [Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again)](/posts/20250619-karpathy-software-changing-again/) — a builder's-side read on the coding-as-leading-edge thread Mollick opens with, where the coder's job shifts from writing code to managing it.
